objectives: Hear /ch/ in initial and final positions of familiar controlled words.
Recognise ch as a two-letter grapheme representing one phoneme in taught words.
Distinguish /ch/ from /sh/ and /t/ in listening contrasts.
Say the target sound without adding an extra vowel.
concepts: A digraph uses two letters to represent one phoneme.
In taught early words, ch can represent /ch/ at the start or end.
The spelling ch can represent other sounds in some words, so learners should follow the taught word pattern and later learn exceptions.
Listening and checking the whole word prevents sound substitutions.

definitions.definition: Two letters working together to represent one phoneme.
The smallest sound unit that can distinguish words.
A letter or group of letters used to represent a sound.

workedExamples.solution: The first sound is /ch/, represented by ch.
The first digraph changes the word and its sound.

commonMistakes: Splitting ch into /t/ and /sh/ during early sound mapping.
Assuming every spelling ch always has the same sound in all English words.
keyTakeaways: In taught words, ch represents one /ch/ phoneme.
Listen for /ch/ at the beginning and end.
Remember that some advanced words use ch differently.
